Only after he truly began working did Zhang Yuansheng understand that “Oilfield Construction Company No. 3” was not merely the name of a work unit.

Behind the name was an entire way of life: what time to leave home in the morning, what kind of people to work with, whom to find first when something went wrong, how far a task had to be carried before it could honestly be called finished. Even the weight of a young man’s words, and where he stood while listening to older colleagues, were being taught all over again.

University had rules too, but student rules were not worker rules. A student’s mistake often ended with a grade, a reprimand, or another attempt. At work, one unfinished thing might already be tied to another person’s time, materials, schedule, and responsibility. A task did not disappear simply because the person handling it was young.
What Zhang Yuansheng first felt was the weight of this fact: unfinished things remain.

Oilfield construction work naturally had the feel of a job site. Projects, equipment, vehicles, materials, and people connected one link to the next. Many things that occupied only a few lines on paper required people in real life to watch, ask, run, and keep following until the pieces met.

As for the exact positions he held in those first years, or every site where he worked, decades later there was no need to force memory into a perfect employment record. What remained was something else: the first realization that work was not a question of “Do I know how?” but “Did this thing finally get done?”
The two questions sound similar. In fact, they are far apart.
“Do I know how?” is mostly about oneself.
“Did it get done?” involves other people.
Zhang Yuansheng began learning to move his attention away from himself.

When a supervisor assigned something, listening to the general idea was not enough. When a colleague pointed out a problem, it could not simply be dismissed as someone else’s concern. When something went wrong at a site, proving it was not your fault could not be the first priority. What slowly allows a person to establish himself in a workplace is often not how much he says, but the quiet knowledge others develop: give this to him, and he will keep carrying it forward.
He was not a young man especially skilled at performing in front of a crowd.

Some new employees quickly became familiar with everyone, talked easily, responded quickly. Zhang Yuansheng was not incapable of that, but his strengths were slower. He tended to watch first, remember what he did not understand, and when something finally came into his hands, work through it piece by piece.
That kind of character is not always noticeable in youth.

A work unit never lacks intelligent people or people who speak well. A newly graduated university student without some spectacular achievement can easily disappear among adults who have already worked for many years. But time has its own sieve. Some people shine at first glance. With others, you discover reliability only after being around them for a long time.
Zhang Yuansheng was closer to the second kind.
He made mistakes too.

No one in his twenties enters a workplace already knowing everything. Often what matures a person is not getting something right the first time, but what he does after getting it wrong. Does he hurry to explain, or first find a way to repair it? Does he push responsibility outward, or remember what happened this time?
Those choices, one by one, formed the earliest colours of his working life.

Many years later, in a Canadian warehouse, when inventory failed to match, goods could not be found, or transfer records became confused, his first reaction would still be to trace where the problem began. Later, he would even turn that habit into Warehouse OS: receiving, transferring, cutting, shipping—each step should leave a trail.
If one insisted on tracing that habit to a single beginning, there probably was no particular day.
It grew slowly out of work like this.
Oilfield life was not only work.

A young person’s world does not suddenly turn grey because he starts receiving wages. After work there were still friends, conversations, gatherings, talk about who was doing what, who might marry soon, who had met someone new. Once the pay truly belonged to him, money acquired a new feeling as well—it could buy things, pay for a meal with friends, and teach him that what came in each month really did have something to do with what went out.
His parents’ way of looking at him slowly changed too.

No matter how grown a child becomes, as long as he is still studying, some part of him remains “not fully established” in his parents’ eyes. After he began working, that layer gradually receded. Family matters began to include his opinion. Relatives no longer asked only how his studies were going; now they asked about work.
“How’s work?”
In China in the 1990s, that question often carried many other questions inside it.
Was the work unit secure? Was the income decent? Was there a future? Where would he live? When would he start a family?
One question nearly contained several of life’s next major events.
Zhang Yuansheng was not in a hurry to design a grand route for his future.

Like most ordinary young people, he began simply by living the days in front of him. He learned the work, income steadied, and little by little he left behind the student air that had clung to him after graduation.
The oilfield changed meaning for him once again.

When he first moved there at twelve, it was the new world his parents had brought him to. When he left at eighteen or nineteen for university, it had become home. When he returned after twenty-four, it became the place where he earned money and carried responsibility for himself.
The same place grows different meanings at different stages of a life.
If his life had continued along that route, it would have made perfect sense.
A work unit, a job, his parents nearby; then marriage, children, and a life growing steadily more settled. For an ordinary person, that was already a complete road.
At the time, Zhang Yuansheng had no particular reason to believe he would one day leave.
Canada was still very far away.
Too far to feel like a decision. It was merely a country on a map.
What began to matter to him was something much closer.
Outside work, another person was beginning to enter his life.

Years later, when he remembered that period, it was difficult to divide “career,” “love,” and “family” into three clean chapters. Real life is never a neatly typeset book. While work is becoming familiar, someone may also be drawing closer. Just as a person learns to carry responsibility in a job, another kind of responsibility may already be waiting nearby.
Some meetings happen without any notification sound.
No one tells you: remember today.
One day you will live with this person, marry her, have a daughter together, and then cross the Pacific side by side.
At that time, Zhang Yuansheng was still only a young employee at Oilfield Construction Company No. 3.
The days were moving forward.
And she was almost there.
